title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Notation as I read it, using the neighbouring pages. X is smooth projective of dimension n over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p. Y is a smooth ample (hyperplane) section and U = X − Y is affine. The objects a^i_{r}, a^i_{a} are codimension-i cycles modulo rational (r) or algebraic (a) equivalence. With the equivalence written as a superscript, a^{r}_i, a^{a}_i are dimension-i cycles. A superscript τ (written Q on the next page) denotes the algebraically trivial part, possibly ⊗Q. E is intersection with the hyperplane class. 'exc. p' means up to p-primary torsion. 'mod gr. finis' means up to finite kernel and cokernel.

Grothendieck is tabulating, dimension by dimension (n = 2 here, n = 3 here and on the next page, n = 4 on the next page), Chow-group analogues of the three Lefschetz theorems. He marks each one 'OK' (known or easy), 'OK si…' (conditional) or '?' (open).
(1) Weak Lefschetz for restriction a^i(X) → a^i(Y) in low codimension.
- n=2: codim 0 trivially; Pic^τ(X) → Pic^τ(Y) injective up to p.
- n=3: Pic(X) → Pic(Y) injective, as in SGA 2 Grothendieck–Lefschetz; Pic^τ bijective up to p, since H^1(X) ≅ H^1(Y).
(2) Gysin direction a_i(Y) → a_i(X) in low dimension.
- n=2: CH_0(Y) → CH_0(X) surjective, and likewise on degree-0 parts. Mod algebraic equivalence, 0-cycles are Z (degree), so the map is bijective.
- n=3: CH_0(Y) → CH_0(X) 'bijective exc. p', with the side condition '2e jacob. int. = jacob. Alb.', i.e. degree-0 0-cycles are parametrised by the Albanese.
- n=3: a^a_1(Y) = NS(Y) → (1-cycles on X mod algebraic equivalence) surjective? — marked '?'.
(2') The affine consequence CH_0(U) = 0. The next page adds A^a_1(U) = 0 '??' for n=3.
(3) Hard Lefschetz E^{n−2i}: a^i_a(X) → a^{n−i}_a(X) up to finite groups.
- n=2: Z → Z (multiplication by H^2) and NS → NS (identity): OK.
- n=3: Z → Z OK. E: NS(X) → a^2_a(X) bijective up to finite groups is labelled 'Conjecture raisonnable', circled '?'. A pencil arrow links it to the '?' of the Gysin surjectivity in (2).
- Hard Lefschetz for the algebraically trivial parts mod rational equivalence. The next page shows the index pattern E^{n+1−2i}: CH^i_alg → CH^{n+1−i}_alg (n=3: CH^1→CH^3 by E^2; n=4: CH^1→CH^4 by E^3, CH^2→CH^3 by E). This is the odd-degree Lefschetz H^{2i−1} → H^{2n+1−2i}.
- For n=2 this amounts to Pic^0(X) → CH_0(X)_alg via E. It holds iff the Albanese kernel vanishes, which is exactly the marginal 'OK si jacobienne int. = jacob. d'Albanese'.

Purpose: to locate precisely which parts of a 'Lefschetz theory for Chow groups' are provable and which reduce to representability, i.e. to 'continuous' questions about intermediate Jacobians versus 'numerical' ones. This sits next to the standard conjectures, of which conjecture B is the cohomological hard Lefschetz.
errors: n=3, (2): 'CH_0(Y) → CH_0(X) bijective exc. p' is false unconditionally. Example: Y a quartic (K3) or higher-degree surface in X = P^3 has an infinite-dimensional CH_0 (Mumford), while CH_0(P^3) = Z. It is only true under the stated representability hypothesis on Y and X. For Y sufficiently ample, p_g(Y) > 0, so that hypothesis always fails (Mumford/Roitman); the conditional statement is essentially vacuous for very ample sections. Injectivity fails on the 'transcendental' graded piece, since H_{n−1}(Y) → H_{n−1}(X) is only surjective.

n=3, (2): 'NS(Y) → (1-cycles on X mod algebraic equivalence) surjective (exc. p)' is false. NS(Y) is finitely generated, while the Griffiths group of a general quintic threefold is nontrivial (Griffiths 1969) and of infinite rank even ⊗Q (Clemens 1983). Grothendieck rightly put '?'. The affine variant A^a_1(U) = 0 on the next page fails for the same reason.

n=3, (3): the 'Conjecture raisonnable' E: NS(X) → CH^2(X)/alg bijective modulo finite groups is false. Griffiths' 1969 example already gives a non-torsion, homologically trivial, algebraically nontrivial 1-cycle on the quintic. It cannot lie in the image of NS ⊗ Q, because E: NS_Q → H^4 is injective by cohomological hard Lefschetz. Clemens shows the cokernel even has infinite rank.

Possible inconsistency or misreading in the n=2 rational-equivalence block. The pattern on the next page (E^{n+1−2i} on algebraically trivial parts) would give for n=2 the maps CH^0_alg → CH^3_alg (both 0) and E: Pic^0 → CH^2_alg. The transcription reads 'a^0_r^τ → a^2' and 'a^1_r^τ →id a^1_r^τ', which does not fit. The marginal condition (intermediate Jacobian = Albanese) fits only the E: Pic^0 → CH_0 reading.

ideas.what: Systematic table of weak-Lefschetz (restriction) and Gysin (pushforward) statements for Chow groups of an ample section, mod rational and mod algebraic equivalence, with torsion caveats in char p
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz-type conjectures for Chow groups (Hartshorne's question; consequences of Bloch–Beilinson / Nori connectivity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hartshorne (1975, 'Equivalence relations on algebraic cycles and subvarieties of small codimension'); later Bloch–Beilinson, Nori (1993), Paranjape (1994)

ideas.what: Hard Lefschetz for cycles modulo algebraic equivalence up to finite groups ('Conjecture raisonnable'), NS(X) → CH^2(X)/alg for threefolds
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz standard conjecture transposed to algebraic equivalence; refuted via the Griffiths group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Analogue of Grothendieck's standard conjecture B; refuted by Griffiths (1969) and Clemens (1983)
ideas.where_published: Standard conjectures (1969) treats only homological/numerical equivalence; unsure whether the algebraic-equivalence version is stated anywhere

ideas.what: Hard Lefschetz on algebraically trivial cycles mod rational equivalence with odd shift, E^{n+1−2i}: CH^i_alg → CH^{n+1−i}_alg; valid for i=1 exactly when CH_0 is Albanese-representable
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz isomorphism on intermediate Jacobians / gr^1 of the Bloch–Beilinson filtration; Bloch's conjecture-type representability condition
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Bloch–Beilinson framework; representability: Mumford (1968), Roitman, Bloch (1975–80)

ideas.what: CH_0(Y) → CH_0(X) surjective for an ample section, hence CH_0(U) = 0 for the affine complement
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz for zero-cycles / vanishing of CH_0 of the affine complement of an ample divisor
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; Bloch's Lectures on algebraic cycles

ideas.what: Weak Lefschetz for Pic (injective for n≥3, bijective on Pic^τ up to p)

missed.claim: Grothendieck (c. 1965–71) formulated, dimension by dimension, a Lefschetz theory for Chow groups. It covers restriction, Gysin pushforward, affine vanishing and hard Lefschetz, mod rational and mod algebraic equivalence. He sorts the open cases into 'continuous' and 'numerical' questions. This predates Hartshorne's 1975 formulation of the Lefschetz question for Chow groups, and the ideas are not credited to him.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority and context. It shows Grothendieck had separated the representability ('intermediate Jacobian = Albanese') obstruction from the numerical one, prefiguring the Bloch–Beilinson graded picture.

missed.claim: He proposed as a 'Conjecture raisonnable' that hard Lefschetz holds modulo algebraic equivalence up to finite groups. He linked it by an arrow to Gysin surjectivity for 1-cycles. Both are now known to fail (Griffiths 1969, Clemens 1983), but the notes leave them open.
missed.quote: a^1_a(X) —E^1→ a^2_a(X) ? bijectif mod. gr. finis — Conjecture "raisonnable"
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This documents that Grothendieck took the algebraic-equivalence analogue of standard conjecture B seriously. It shows the Griffiths group was the decisive counterexample to a conjecture he considered plausible — a small but genuine point for the history of the standard conjectures.

missed.claim: The correct indexing for hard Lefschetz on algebraically trivial cycles is the odd shift E^{n+1−2i}. He states its validity for 0-cycles on surfaces exactly in terms of Albanese-representability. This explicitly ties Lefschetz-type statements for Chow groups to Bloch's conjecture and Mumford's infinite-dimensionality.
missed.quote: O.K. si jacobienne int. = jacob. d'Albanese
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is the same insight later organised via the Bloch–Beilinson filtration and motives: Lefschetz holds on gr^1 but fails on higher graded pieces. It is not new mathematically, but it shows an early awareness of the structure.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a systematic, early (pre-Hartshorne, roughly contemporary with Mumford) table of Lefschetz conjectures for Chow groups. It includes a named 'Conjecture raisonnable' that was later refuted by Griffiths and Clemens, which is of historical interest. However, no correct new result is lost, and the ideas were later developed independently.
transcription_corrections: Top crossed-out line likely reads '1) dim ≠ n=2' or similar; it is irrelevant.
Margin at n=2 (2): reads roughly 'dans un cas 2 : jacob. int. de 0-cycles = jacob. d'Albanese' — i.e. a representability condition on 0-cycles.

In the n=2 rational-equivalence hard-Lefschetz block, the indices are uncertain. By analogy with the next page (E^{n+1−2i}) one expects CH^0_alg → CH^3_alg (both 0) and Pic^0 → CH^2_alg via E, rather than 'a^1_r^τ →id a^1_r^τ'; check the image.
Pencil margin near n=3 (3): likely 'mod groupes finis' (or 'second/sauf groupes finis'), not 'second groupes finis' as a phrase.
The circled '?' at the bottom carries the label 'Conjecture "raisonnable"'. A pencil arrow links it to the '?' after 'a^a_1(Y) → a^a_1(X) surjectif exc. p'.
'a^a_1' in n=3 (2): superscript a (algebraic equivalence), subscript 1 (dimension 1).
